etymology: English surname Kent, from the ancient county; the given name John from Hebrew Yochanan, “the LORD is gracious.”
biblical_def: John Kent (1766–1843) was a Devonshire shipwright who, unschooled in the academies yet deeply taught in the school of grace, poured out some of the most God-exalting hymnody the Particular Baptists produced. Labouring at Plymouth Dock with his hands, he laboured also in the sanctuary of his heart, and his Gospel Hymns breathe an unashamed sovereign-grace theology: election, particular redemption, the everlasting covenant, and the immutable love of the Father are not merely doctrines he confessed but the very marrow of his song. “Sovereign grace o’er sin abounding” remains his most enduring line, and in it we hear the whole system of the gospel compressed into praise. Kent did not sentimentalize the cross; he magnified it as the ground of the believer’s security, tracing salvation back to the counsel of God before the world began and forward to the glory that shall not fade. He wrote as one who knew himself a debtor to mercy alone, and his verse invites the trembling saint to rest wholly upon a finished work. That a working man with hammer and adze should leave the church such treasure is itself a testimony that the LORD hides these things from the wise and reveals them unto babes, and that the Spirit is no respecter of learning where He purposes to give a singing heart.
webster_summary: English Particular Baptist hymnwriter (1766–1843) whose sovereign-grace hymns magnify electing love and the everlasting covenant.
webster_full: A Devonshire shipwright and self-taught hymnwriter among the Particular Baptists.
Author of the collection Gospel Hymns, marked throughout by high Calvinistic doctrine.
Best known for “Sovereign grace o’er sin abounding,” a hymn of the everlasting covenant.
A layman whose verse magnified election, particular redemption, and the immutable love of God.
A witness that saving song may flow from the workbench as truly as from the pulpit.

corruption_summary: A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers the principle of sovereign grace magnified in worship.
corruption_paragraphs: John Kent is preserved not because his name is disputed but because his song refuses the age its two favourite errors: that grace is a reward for the willing and that worship is a mood we manufacture. Kent sang the covenant as a thing settled in eternity, and such singing rebukes every gospel that makes the sinner the first cause of his own salvation.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that congregational praise must be doctrinally weighty—that the church sings her theology and so preaches to herself. Where hymnody is drained of election, atonement, and covenant, it becomes flattery of the worshipper rather than adoration of the LORD. Kent’s verse calls us back to a praise that is Godward, cross-centred, and grounded in immutable love.
roots_summary: Kent’s hymnody roots the church’s worship in the eternal covenant of grace and the doctrines of sovereign mercy.

The dignity of lay labour offered up in worship as a fragrant sacrifice of song.

etymology: Surname Grigg, a diminutive form of Gregory (Greek Grēgorios, “watchful”); Joseph from Hebrew, “he shall add.”
biblical_def: Joseph Grigg (c. 1720–1768) rose from a mechanic’s trade to the Presbyterian ministry, serving as assistant at Silver Street Chapel in London before an early retirement to writing and quiet devotion. Yet the LORD had ordained that a hymn composed, by tradition, when Grigg was but a boy of ten should outlive every sermon he preached. “Jesus, and shall it ever be, a mortal man ashamed of Thee?” is the cry of a soul that reckons the fear of man a shameful thing and the confession of Christ the highest honour a creature can bear. In an age that prizes reputation above obedience, Grigg’s hymn presses upon the conscience that unbelief blushes at its Saviour while faith glories in Him. The verse rises to holy resolve—“Ashamed of Jesus! that dear Friend on whom my hopes of heaven depend”—and closes in the assurance that He who is not ashamed to call His people brethren will one day own them before the Father and the holy angels. Grigg wrote also “Behold a Stranger at the door,” a tender pleading with the Christless heart. His life reminds the church that a single Spirit-borne stanza, faithfully framed, may do more for Christ than a lifetime of applause, and that boldness in confession is the badge of every true disciple.
webster_summary: English hymnwriter (c. 1720–1768), author of “Jesus, and Shall It Ever Be,” a hymn against shame in confessing Christ.
webster_full: An English minister who rose from a mechanic’s trade to Presbyterian ministry in London.
Assistant at Silver Street Chapel before retiring to writing and devotion.
Author of “Jesus, and Shall It Ever Be,” a hymn resolving never to be ashamed of Christ.
Also wrote “Behold a Stranger at the Door,” pleading with the unconverted.
A witness that bold confession, not the fear of man, marks the true disciple.

corruption_summary: A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his hymn recovers the principle of unashamed confession of Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: Grigg is preserved because his single great hymn names the sin the age most flatters: the shame that blushes to own the Lord Jesus before a scoffing world. Where the church trims her confession to purchase the world’s good opinion, Grigg’s stanza indicts her, for to be ashamed of Christ is already to be counted with the adulterous generation.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is bold, open confession—that the disciple who is not ashamed of Christ shall find that Christ is not ashamed of him. In a day of quiet, apologetic Christianity, Grigg summons the believer to reckon the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of men, and to fear the shame of that great day more than the frowns of this present one.
roots_summary: Grigg’s hymn roots Christian courage in Christ’s own promise to confess those who confess Him.

etymology: Benjamin, Hebrew “son of the right hand”; Francis, from the Latin Franciscus, “Frenchman, freeman.”
biblical_def: Benjamin Francis (1734–1799) was a Welshman of Newcastle Emlyn, converted young and called to the Particular Baptist ministry, who for over forty years pastored the church at Horsley in Gloucestershire and itinerated tirelessly through the western counties. A preacher of uncommon warmth and a poet in both English and his native Welsh, he laboured in an era when the Baptists were emerging from a season of deadness into the fresh life of evangelical zeal, and he was among those who fanned the flame. So esteemed was his gospel labour that he was thrice invited to great London pulpits, and thrice he refused, judging his little country flock a nobler charge than the applause of the city—a choice that rebukes every minister who measures his call by the size of his hearers. His hymns and elegies, many in Welsh, stirred the affections of the chapels, and his preaching bore fruit in conversions and in churches planted. Francis wrote a moving elegy on the death of George Whitefield, joining his voice to the mourning of the awakened church. His life embodies the pastoral fidelity the Scriptures commend: content in an obscure vineyard, fervent in the pulpit, prolific with the pen, and jealous only for the honour of his Master. He stands as a Welsh forefather of the missionary awakening soon to break upon the Baptists through Carey and his circle.
webster_summary: Welsh Particular Baptist pastor and hymnwriter (1734–1799) who declined London for a faithful country ministry.
webster_full: A Welsh Particular Baptist minister born at Newcastle Emlyn.
Pastor at Horsley, Gloucestershire, for over forty years, and a tireless itinerant.
A hymnwriter and poet in both English and Welsh who stirred the chapels.
Thrice declined prominent London pulpits to keep his country flock.
A forerunner of the Baptist missionary awakening in the western counties.
scriptures: Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful.

corruption_summary: A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers the principle of pastoral contentment in an obscure charge.
corruption_paragraphs: Francis is preserved because his thrice-refused London pulpit exposes an idol the age still bows to: the notion that a ministry’s worth is weighed by its platform. He judged a hidden Gloucestershire flock a richer stewardship than the applause of the metropolis, and so preached with his feet a sermon the ambitious sorely need.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is faithfulness in the appointed vineyard—that the LORD requires stewards to be found faithful, not famous. Francis’s song and his sacrifice call the church back to a ministry measured by love for Christ’s sheep rather than the size of the crowd, and to the sowing of precious seed that returns, in God’s time, with sheaves of rejoicing.
roots_summary: Francis’s ministry roots the pastoral office in faithful stewardship and love for the flock over worldly advancement.
roots_lines: The steward’s one requirement, that he “be found faithful” (1Co 4:2).

The Welsh chapels’ awakening as seedbed of the coming missionary zeal.

etymology: Thomas, from Aramaic tē’ōmā, “twin”; Olivers, a Welsh surname derived from Oliver, from the olive, emblem of peace.
biblical_def: Thomas Olivers (1725–1799) was a Welsh orphan and profligate shoemaker whose riotous youth was arrested by the preaching of George Whitefield on the text, “Is not this a brand plucked out of the fire?” Wondrously converted, this brand became a burning and shining lamp: he cast in his lot with the Methodist awakening and travelled long years as one of Wesley’s itinerant preachers, wearing out his life upon the road for the gospel that had rescued him. Yet Olivers is remembered chiefly for a hymn born of the synagogue and the sanctuary. Hearing the Hebrew doxology the Yigdal sung in a London synagogue, he took its ancient frame and filled it with pure Christian praise, producing “The God of Abraham praise, who reigns enthroned above.” The hymn adores the great I AM, the covenant God of the patriarchs, now confessed as the Triune LORD who has sworn by Himself and will not fail His people. Its majestic close—“I shall behold His face, I shall His power adore”—lifts the singer to the very courts of glory. That a plucked brand should frame a hymn adoring the God of Abraham is itself a parable of grace: the LORD stoops to the vilest and makes him a herald of His covenant faithfulness to a thousand generations.
webster_summary: Welsh Methodist itinerant preacher (1725–1799), author of “The God of Abraham Praise.”
webster_full: A Welsh orphan and shoemaker converted under Whitefield’s preaching.
A long-serving itinerant preacher among the Wesleyan Methodists.
Author of “The God of Abraham Praise,” framed on the Hebrew Yigdal.
A “brand plucked out of the fire” who became a herald of covenant grace.
A hymnwriter who filled an ancient Jewish doxology with Christian adoration.

Exo 3:6

Heb 6:13

corruption_summary: A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his hymn recovers the adoration of the covenant God of Abraham.
corruption_paragraphs: Olivers is preserved because his hymn holds forth what a rootless age most needs: the great I AM, the covenant God of the patriarchs, who swore by Himself and cannot lie. Where worship drifts toward a vague and manageable deity, “The God of Abraham Praise” recalls the church to the awful, unchanging God who chose Jerusalem and keeps His oath.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the adoration of God as He has revealed Himself—the eternal, self-existent LORD, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, now confessed as the Holy Trinity. Olivers’s own rescue, a brand plucked from the fire, preaches that this God stoops to the perishing; his hymn preaches that the rescued must adore Him with reverence and godly fear.
roots_summary: Olivers’s hymn roots Christian praise in the covenant name and oath of the God of Abraham.
roots_lines: The brand “plucked out of the fire” as an emblem of sovereign rescue (Zec 3:2).
God’s self-naming as “the God of Abraham, of Isaac, and of Jacob” (Exo 3:6).
The divine oath sworn by God upon Himself to Abraham (Heb 6:13).
The revelation of the incommunicable name, “I AM THAT I AM” (Exo 3:14).
The framing of ancient Hebrew doxology into full Christian, Trinitarian praise.

etymology: Edward, Old English “rich guard”; Perronet, a French Huguenot surname, marking the family’s descent from Protestant refugees.
biblical_def: Edward Perronet (1721–1792) sprang from a family of French Huguenot stock; his father Vincent, the godly vicar of Shoreham, was so trusted a counsellor of the Wesleys as to be called “the Archbishop of Methodism.” Edward laboured in the early Methodist awakening and endured its perils, being roughly handled by mobs for the gospel’s sake, before conscience over the sacraments led him at length to an independent ministry and a small congregation at Canterbury. Yet the whole church remembers him for one soaring hymn: “All hail the power of Jesus’ name! Let angels prostrate fall; bring forth the royal diadem, and crown Him Lord of all.” No hymn in the English tongue more gloriously summons the whole creation—angels, martyrs, ransomed Israel, Gentile sinners, and “every kindred, every tribe”—to the coronation of the Lord Jesus Christ. It is the church’s answer to the vision of the throne, where the Lamb receives the crowns of all the redeemed. Perronet, who suffered stripes for that Name, framed the very anthem in which the ages shall hail its power. His hymn preaches the universal, cosmic lordship of Christ and the final gathering of a people out of every nation to fall before Him; it is a hymn to be sung on the knees of the heart, in glad anticipation of the day when we shall crown Him Lord of all.
webster_summary: English hymnwriter of Huguenot descent (1721–1792), author of “All Hail the Power of Jesus’ Name.”
webster_full: An English preacher of French Huguenot descent, son of Vincent Perronet of Shoreham.
A labourer in the early Methodist awakening who suffered mob violence for the gospel.
Later an independent minister with a small congregation at Canterbury.
Author of “All Hail the Power of Jesus’ Name,” the great coronation hymn.
A herald of the universal lordship of Christ over every kindred and tribe.

corruption_summary: A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his hymn recovers the universal crown-rights of the Lord Jesus Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: Perronet is preserved because his hymn confesses the very truth a self-crowning age denies: that Jesus alone is Lord of all, before whom every knee must bow. Where the world would enthrone the sovereign self, “All Hail the Power” brings forth the royal diadem for another Head, and summons angels and nations alike to prostrate homage.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the crown-rights of Christ—His exaltation to the name above every name and His right to the worship of every tribe. Perronet, who bore stripes for that Name, teaches the church that to hail its power is no idle song but a pledge of allegiance; the hymn is a rehearsal on earth of the coronation the redeemed shall consummate in glory.
roots_summary: Perronet’s hymn roots the church’s praise in the exaltation and universal reign of the crucified Lamb.

The gathering of “every kindred, every tribe” to the coronation of Christ.

etymology: Bakewell, an English place-name in Derbyshire, “Badeca’s spring or well”; John, Hebrew, “the LORD is gracious.”
biblical_def: John Bakewell (1721–1819) was a Derbyshire man awakened in his youth by reading Boston’s Fourfold State, that great Puritan anatomy of sin and grace, and thereafter a lay preacher associated with the Methodist revival who lived to the great age of ninety-eight. His long life was one continued testimony to the keeping power of God, and his epitaph, penned by himself, confessed that he had “adorned the doctrine of God our Saviour for above sixty years.” Yet his enduring memorial is the hymn “Hail, Thou once despised Jesus! Hail, Thou Galilean King!” It is a hymn of the great exchange, tracing the Saviour from His humiliation—despised, rejected, bearing our sin, made a curse, dying to set us free—to His exaltation at the Father’s right hand as our all-prevailing Intercessor. Bakewell gathers the whole gospel into its stanzas: the atonement finished, the wrath appeased, the throne of grace opened, and the ransomed church joining the everlasting song, “Worthy the Lamb.” The hymn moves the affections from the shame of the cross to the splendour of the crown, teaching the believer to hail the very Christ the world despised. In Bakewell’s long and steadfast course, and in this hymn of the despised and exalted King, the church beholds a life and a song both wholly given to magnify the Lamb once slain and now reigning.
webster_summary: English Methodist lay preacher and hymnwriter (1721–1819), author of “Hail, Thou Once Despised Jesus.”
webster_full: A Derbyshire man awakened through Thomas Boston’s Fourfold State.
A lay preacher of the Methodist revival who lived to ninety-eight.
Author of “Hail, Thou Once Despised Jesus,” a hymn of humiliation and exaltation.

A witness of long perseverance who adorned the gospel above sixty years.

corruption_summary: A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his hymn recovers the once-despised and now-exalted Christ of substitution.
corruption_paragraphs: Bakewell is preserved because his hymn confesses the very Christ the world still despises: the crucified Substitute made a curse for sinners. Where the age craves a Jesus without a cross, “Hail, Thou Once Despised Jesus” holds forth the man of sorrows who bore our sin and now pleads our cause, and bids the church hail Him whom men esteemed not.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is penal substitution and the intercession of the exalted Christ—that He was made a curse for us and ever liveth to save to the uttermost. Bakewell’s hymn, and his sixty years of adorning that gospel, summon the believer to trace the whole way from the shame of Calvary to the throne of grace, and there to worship the Lamb once slain.
roots_summary: Bakewell’s hymn roots the gospel in Christ’s substitutionary curse-bearing and His unceasing intercession.

etymology: Spilsbury, an English place-name surname (Oxfordshire); John, Hebrew Yochanan, “the LORD is gracious.”
biblical_def: John Spilsbury (c. 1593–c. 1668) was, by the best account, the pastor of the first Particular Baptist congregation in England, gathered in London about the year 1638 out of the separatist churches, when a company of believers, persuaded from Scripture that baptism belongs to disciples and not to infants, resolved to obey their Lord in the ordinance He appointed. A cobbler by trade and a labourer in the Word, Spilsbury led this flock to recover believers’ baptism at a time when to do so was to court reproach, ejection, and peril. He set his convictions in print, defending in his treatise on the ordinance that the subjects of baptism are professing believers and its true mode a burial with Christ, answering with Scripture those who pressed the baptism of infants. These first Particular Baptists were Calvinistic to the bone, and from their number and their confessions would flow, in the next generation, the great Second London Confession of 1689 which the churches own to this day. Spilsbury stands therefore as a forefather of the whole Reformed Baptist people: a man who counted obedience to Christ’s plain command dearer than the peace of conformity, and who, gathering a church upon the rule of the Word, planted a seed from which a mighty tree of confessing, baptizing, gospel-preaching congregations has grown.
webster_summary: Pastor (c. 1593–c. 1668) of the first Particular Baptist congregation, gathered in London about 1638.
webster_full: The reputed pastor of England’s first Particular (Calvinistic) Baptist church.

A cobbler by trade who recovered believers’ baptism from Scripture.
Author of a treatise defending baptism as the ordinance of professing disciples.

corruption_summary: A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his labour recovers the ordinance of believers’ baptism.
corruption_paragraphs: Spilsbury is preserved because he stood, at cost, upon the plain command of Christ: that baptism follows faith and pictures a burial with the risen Lord. Where the churches of his day pressed the baptism of unconscious infants, he gathered a people to obey the Great Commission as it is written, teaching the nations and baptizing the taught.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is believers’ baptism—that the ordinance belongs to those who gladly receive the word, and signifies death to sin and newness of life in Christ. Spilsbury’s courage summons the churches to prize obedience to Scripture above the comfort of custom, and to guard the ordinances Christ Himself appointed as the badges of a professing, regenerate church.
roots_summary: Spilsbury’s ministry roots the Baptist confession in the scriptural recovery of believers’ baptism.

etymology: Samuel, Hebrew “asked of God” or “heard of God”; Pearce, an English surname, a variant of Piers or Peter, “rock.”
biblical_def: Samuel Pearce (1766–1799) was pastor of the Cannon Street Baptist Church in Birmingham and one of the brightest lights of the Baptist missionary awakening, so eminent for holy love that he was called by his brethren “the seraphic Pearce.” Converted as a youth and trained at Bristol, he entered the ministry with a heart aflame for the salvation of the heathen, and when the Baptist Missionary Society was formed in 1792 with Carey, Fuller, Sutcliff, and Ryland, Pearce cast himself wholly into the cause. He longed to go to India himself, and offered, but the Society judged his gifts too precious to spare from home; he bowed to their counsel as to the will of God and laboured instead as an eloquent pleader for the mission, a raiser of funds, and a stirrer of prayer. His letters and diaries, published after his early death from consumption at thirty-three, breathe such nearness to Christ and such flame of devotion that they have kindled the affections of the church ever since. Andrew Fuller wrote his memoir that others might catch his fire. Pearce’s brief course preaches that the measure of a life is not its length but its love, and that a man wholly given to Christ, whether he crosses the sea or pleads at home, may set a whole generation alight for the gospel of the nations.
webster_summary: Baptist minister (1766–1799), “the seraphic Pearce,” a burning light of Carey’s missionary circle.
webster_full: Pastor of Cannon Street Baptist Church, Birmingham.

Also I heard the voice of the Lord, saying, Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? Then said I, Here am I; send me.
corruption_summary: A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers the principle of Christ-constrained missionary love.
corruption_paragraphs: Pearce is preserved because his “seraphic” devotion rebukes an age content with a cool and calculating religion. His heart was so warmed by the love of Christ that it overflowed toward the perishing heathen, and even when denied the mission field he coveted, he burned no less brightly for the sending of others.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the constraining love of Christ that makes a soul long for the salvation of the nations—“here am I; send me.” Pearce teaches that submission to God’s ordering of one’s calling is no cooling of zeal but its purification, and that a brief life wholly aflame for Christ may kindle the missionary fervour of a whole generation.
roots_summary: Pearce’s life roots missionary zeal in the constraining love of Christ and glad submission to God’s call.
roots_lines: The single-eyed confession, “to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Php 1:21).
The sending of preachers with beautiful feet of good tidings (Rom 10:15).
The love of Christ that “constraineth us” toward the lost (2Co 5:14).
The prophet’s ready answer, “Here am I; send me” (Isa 6:8).
The founding of the Baptist Missionary Society as fruit of such love.
usage: “Fuller’s memoir of Pearce set many a young minister ablaze.”
“They called him the seraphic Pearce for his flame of holy love.”
“Denied India, he pleaded the mission’s cause at home with all his heart.”

etymology: Sutcliff, a Yorkshire place-name surname, “south cliff”; John, Hebrew Yochanan, “the LORD is gracious.”
biblical_def: John Sutcliff (1752–1814) was the Particular Baptist pastor of Olney in Buckinghamshire, that same village hallowed by John Newton and William Cowper, and one of the chief instruments in the reviving of the Baptist churches from spiritual deadness. Reading Jonathan Edwards’ Humble Attempt, which called the churches to united, extraordinary prayer for the outpouring of the Spirit, Sutcliff was so stirred that in 1784 he moved the Northamptonshire Association to establish a monthly concert of prayer—the Prayer Call for “the revival of real religion, and the extension of Christ’s kingdom.” This humble covenant to plead with God, spreading through the associations, is reckoned by many the seedbed from which the Baptist Missionary Society sprang in 1792 and Carey was sent to India. Sutcliff thus stands as a father of the modern missionary movement, not chiefly by preaching or by sailing, but by summoning the churches to their knees; he believed with all his heart that the LORD would be enquired of by His people to do these things for them, and that prayer is the appointed forerunner of every awakening. His life preaches that the great works of God begin in the closet and the prayer-meeting, and that the church that would see the kingdom advance must first agree together to ask.
webster_summary: Particular Baptist pastor of Olney (1752–1814) who spread the Prayer Call for revival and missions.
webster_full: The Particular Baptist pastor of Olney, Buckinghamshire.
Stirred by Edwards’ Humble Attempt to call the churches to united prayer.
Moved the 1784 Prayer Call for the revival of religion and Christ’s kingdom.
A chief instrument in the awakening that produced the Baptist Missionary Society.
A father of modern missions who summoned the churches to their knees.
scriptures: Thus saith the Lord GOD; I will yet for this be enquired of by the house of Israel, to do it for them; I will increase them with men like a flock.
Zec 8:21
And the inhabitants of one city shall go to another, saying, Let us go speedily to pray before the LORD, and to seek the LORD of hosts: I will go also.
Act 1:14
These all continued with one accord in prayer and supplication, with the women, and Mary the mother of Jesus, and with his brethren.
Luk 18:1
And he spake a parable unto them to this end, that men ought always to pray, and not to faint;
corruption_summary: A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his labour recovers the principle of united prayer as the forerunner of revival.
corruption_paragraphs: Sutcliff is preserved because he recovered a truth a busy and self-reliant age forgets: that the LORD ordains to be enquired of by His people, and that the great advances of the kingdom are born in the prayer-meeting. His Prayer Call bound the churches together to plead for the Spirit, and God answered by opening the door to the nations.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is united, extraordinary prayer—that men ought always to pray and not to faint, and that revival and missions alike wait upon the church’s agreement to seek the LORD of hosts. Sutcliff teaches that no scheme or strategy can supply the place of prayer, and that the humble concert of the saints on their knees is the appointed forerunner of every outpouring of grace.
roots_summary: Sutcliff’s Prayer Call roots revival and missions in the united, importunate prayer of the churches.
roots_lines: The LORD’s ordinance to be “enquired of” before He acts for His people (Eze 36:37).
The summons, “Let us go speedily to pray before the LORD” (Zec 8:21).
The disciples continuing “with one accord in prayer and supplication” (Act 1:14).
The duty always to pray and not to faint (Luk 18:1).
The 1784 Prayer Call as the seedbed of the Baptist Missionary Society.
usage: “Sutcliff’s 1784 Prayer Call went before Carey’s sending to India.”
“He was stirred by Edwards’ Humble Attempt to concerted prayer.”
“The pastor of Olney called the churches to plead for revival.”

etymology: George, from Greek Geōrgios, “husbandman, tiller of the soil”; Liele (also spelled Lisle), the surname borne from his former condition of bondage.
biblical_def: George Liele (c. 1750–1820) was born a slave in Virginia and converted in Georgia under the preaching of the gospel, whereupon his master, discerning the grace of God upon him, freed him that he might preach. Liele became one of the first ordained black Baptist preachers in America and gathered congregations of the enslaved and the free before, in the upheavals of the War of Independence, he departed for Jamaica about 1782. There, a labouring man tilling the field the LORD had given him, he preached Christ to the slaves of the island, baptized his converts, and gathered at Kingston what is reckoned among the first Baptist churches in Jamaica—doing this a full decade before William Carey sailed for India, so that Liele stands as the first American Baptist missionary to carry the gospel abroad, and that a freed slave. He supported himself by his own labour, drew up a covenant for his church, suffered imprisonment and opposition, yet held forth the word of life to a people in bondage far greater than any chain. His life is a marvel of sovereign grace: that the LORD should take a man from slavery, give him liberty in Christ, and send him across the sea as a herald of the gospel before the celebrated missions began. Liele preaches that the good news knows no bound of station or colour, and that whom the Son makes free is free indeed to spend himself for the salvation of others.
webster_summary: Freed slave (c. 1750–1820), first American Baptist missionary, who carried the gospel to Jamaica.
webster_full: Born a slave in Virginia, converted in Georgia, and freed to preach the gospel.
One of the first ordained black Baptist preachers in America.
Departed for Jamaica about 1782 and gathered a Baptist church at Kingston.
Reckoned the first American Baptist missionary, preceding Carey by a decade.
A self-supporting herald who preached Christ to the enslaved of the island.
scriptures: Joh 8:36
If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed.
Gal 3:28
There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus.
Act 8:4
Therefore they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word.
Princes shall come out of Egypt; Ethiopia shall soon stretch out her hands unto God.
corruption_summary: A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers the principle of the gospel’s freedom crossing every bound.
corruption_paragraphs: Liele is preserved because his story confesses the true liberty a confused age counterfeits: that whom the Son makes free is free indeed, though his body wore a chain. Freed to preach, he did not squander his liberty upon himself but spent it crossing the sea to carry Christ to others yet in bondage, and so preached freedom of the deepest kind.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the gospel’s indifference to station and its power to save out of every people—in Christ neither bond nor free, but all one. Liele, a freed slave and the first American Baptist missionary, teaches that the LORD delights to take the lowly and make them heralds, and that the truly free man is the one whom Christ has liberated to spend himself for the salvation of the perishing.
roots_summary: Liele’s mission roots the spread of the gospel in Christ’s liberating grace reaching every people and place.
roots_lines: The Son’s liberty, “ye shall be free indeed” (Joh 8:36).
The oneness in Christ of “bond nor free” alike (Gal 3:28).
The scattered saints who “went every where preaching the word” (Act 8:4).
The prophecy that Ethiopia shall “stretch out her hands unto God” (Psa 68:31).
The sending of a freed slave abroad a decade before Carey.
usage: “George Liele preached in Jamaica ten years before Carey reached India.”
“Freed to preach, he became the first American Baptist missionary.”
“He gathered a Baptist church at Kingston among the enslaved.”
